beats.headline: Why do your unit tests pass while production breaks?
beats.subline: Handwritten mocks drift from reality. Here is why your microservice integration strategy is likely lying to you.
beats.narration: Your unit tests pass against a hardcoded mock. Then the provider team renames a field, and your production service crashes. This is mock drift. Let's fix it with Consumer-Driven Contract Testing.

beats.title: Mocking vs. Contract Testing
beats.narration: Handwritten mocks are just guesses. Pact creates a shared contract file. The consumer records the expectation, and the provider replays that exact request against its live code to prove compatibility.

beats.title: The Pact Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Consumer defines, Provider verifies
beats.narration: The consumer generates a JSON pact file. It lands in the Pact Broker. The provider then downloads it and replays the request against its actual Spring Boot controller. If it fails, the build breaks.

beats.title: Using LambdaDsl for Flexibility

steps.explanation: Don't hardcode IDs. Match the format so the provider can return any valid UUID.
Use regex to ensure the provider only returns allowed status strings.

beats.narration: Avoid hardcoding values. Use LambdaDsl matchers for UUIDs and dates. This keeps your contract flexible while still enforcing the exact structure your consumer code expects.

beats.headline: How do you test a provider that needs data?
beats.subline: Pact's @State annotation is the secret sauce for seeding your database before verification.
beats.narration: Your provider API needs a database record to exist before it can return a 200. How do you handle that in a CI pipeline? Meet the @State annotation.

beats.title: Seeding State with @State

steps.explanation: Pact calls this before replaying the HTTP request. Seed your DB here.
Crucial! Clean up state so tests don't leak into each other.

beats.narration: The consumer defines the state name. The provider implements it. Use SETUP to seed your database via Testcontainers, and always use TEARDOWN to wipe it clean. No state leakage allowed.

beats.narration: Don't just run tests locally. Pass these JVM flags in your CI to publish verification results back to the Pact Broker. Now the Broker knows exactly which versions are compatible.

beats.title: Pact vs. OpenAPI
beats.narration: OpenAPI tells you what an API offers. Pact tells you what it actually needs. If a field isn't in a Pact contract, you can safely delete it without breaking anyone.

beats.headline: Can you contract test an event-driven system?
beats.subline: Kafka schemas break just as silently as REST APIs. Here is how to lock them down.
beats.narration: Kafka is just a pipe. If you rename a field in your JSON event, your downstream consumer dies. Pact handles this with Message Contracts, no Kafka broker required.

beats.title: Verifying Kafka Producers

steps.explanation: Pact calls this method to get the event payload for verification.
Return bytes plus headers to simulate the real Kafka message structure.

beats.narration: The provider uses @PactVerifyProvider. It returns the raw bytes and headers of your event. Pact validates this against the consumer's expected schema. No Kafka broker needed for the test.

beats.title: Async Verification Flow
beats.narration: The consumer defines the schema. The provider serializes its real POJO. Pact compares the two. If your POJO changes and breaks the schema, the test fails before you even touch Kafka.

beats.title: Sync vs. Async Contracts
beats.narration: HTTP contracts focus on status codes and paths. Message contracts focus purely on the payload schema and headers. Both prevent breaking changes in your distributed system.

beats.headline: How do you prevent a bad deploy?
beats.subline: The Pact Broker's compatibility matrix is the final gatekeeper for your microservices.
beats.narration: You have the contracts. Now, how do you stop a breaking change from hitting production? You need the Pact Broker's compatibility matrix.

beats.title: The can-i-deploy Command
beats.caption: The most important command in your pipeline
beats.narration: Before you deploy, run this. It checks if your version is compatible with every consumer currently in production. If it fails, the pipeline stops. Zero breaking changes reach your users.

beats.title: Deployment Gating
beats.narration: The Broker acts as a gatekeeper. It knows what is running in production. If your new version breaks a live consumer, the Broker returns exit code one, and your deploy is blocked.

beats.title: Recording Deployment
beats.caption: Update the Broker after rollout
beats.narration: After a successful rollout, record the deployment. The Broker needs to know what is live to accurately gate future releases. This completes the feedback loop.

takeaways: Broker is your source of truth
